subject: Estimation Time for Multilevel Model: JAGS v. STAN

messages.author: 211887b39a900c7d
messages.subject: Estimation Time for Multilevel Model: JAGS v. STAN
parts:
I’ve heard some great things about STAN in terms of the speed of reaching convergence and sampling. With that, I compared STAN to JAGS to fit a multilevel growth model. The posteriors obtained from both programs were very similar. With STAN, clear evidence of convergence for two chains was present with a warm-up of 500 iterations and 1000 additional iterations with no thinning to construct the posterior. With JAGS, I ran two chains for 2000 burnin iterations and 4500 additional iterations with a thinning interval of 15. JAGS took just less than one minute and STAN took about 4.5 minutes. Given what I have heard about the speed of STAN, this was a very surprising result, especially given that fewer iterations were required to reach convergence than with JAGS. Any ideas about why I’m seeing such a difference in speed in favor of JAGS would be greatly appreciated. The amount of time taken per dataset is key as the chosen program will be used for a simulation study. The program is provided below; any input about any inefficiencies are welcome.

 

data {

  int<lower=0> N; // Number of subjects.

  int<lower=0> J; // Number of measurement occasions.

  real y[N,J]; // Dimensions of the observed data.

  vector [J] time; // Balanced coding of time (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)

  cov_matrix[2] Omega; // Diagonal matrix on growth params (prior).

}

 

parameters {

  vector[2] beta[N]; // level-1 growth parameters.

  vector[2] gamma; // level-2 intercept and linear parameters.

  real gamma20; // level-2 quadratic parameter.

  real<lower=.001> resvar; // homoskedastics residual variance

  cov_matrix[2] psi; // covariance matrix among growth parameters.

}

 

transformed parameters {

  // real rho;

  real<lower=.001> ressd; // standard deviation of residuals

  //rho <- psi[1,2]/sqrt(psi[1,1]*psi[2,2]);

  ressd <- sqrt(resvar);

}

 

model {

  resvar ~ inv_gamma(.001,.001); // residual variance prior.

  gamma ~ normal(0,1000); // diffuse prior on intercept and linear growth params.

  gamma20 ~ normal(0,1000); // diffuse prior on quadratic growth param

  psi ~ inv_wishart(2,Omega); // prior on intercept and linear covariance matrix

 

  for(i in 1:N){

    beta[i] ~ multi_normal(gamma,psi); // prior on level-1 intercept and linear growth params.

    for(j in 1:J){

      y[i,j] ~ normal(beta[i,1]+beta[i,2]*time[j]+gamma20*(time[j]*time[j]), resvar); // growth model.

    }

  }

}

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: Estimation Time for Multilevel Model: JAGS v. STAN
parts:
Hi Derek,

You will want to compare number of effective samples per second or seconds per effective sample, rather than total running time. Also, if you are repeatedly fitting the same model to different datasets, you only have to compile the stan model once.

You can improve the speed of the stan model by vectorizing the sampling statements. See below; I vectorized things over N, assuming that N>J. If J>N, it would be more efficient to vectorize over J. See below for the vectorized code.

Note that univariate normal distributions in Stan are defined with standard deviation, not variance.

You can move things that are not used in the model to the generated quantities block (rho in this case), so they aren't recalculated for every leapfrog step (everything in the parameters, transformed parameters, and the model blocks is executed/calculated for every leapfrog step in the discrete HMC simulation).

Last, there are a few people around here that like to stay away from gamma and inverse wishart priors (I'll leave it to them to explain it, they'll do a much better job at it). For the bivariate normal case, you're probably better off modeling standard errors and correlation as separate parameters.

Best,

Luc

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

data {
  int<lower=0> N;           // Number of subjects.
  int<lower=0> J;           // Number of measurement occasions.
vector[N] y[J];           // Dimensions of the observed data.

vector[J] time;           // Balanced coding of time (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)
  cov_matrix[2] Omega;      // Diagonal matrix on growth params (prior).
}

parameters {
  vector[2] beta[N];        // level-1 growth parameters.
  vector[2] gamma;          // level-2 intercept and linear parameters.
  real gamma20;             // level-2 quadratic parameter.
real<lower=.001> ressd;   // homoskedastics residual variance

cov_matrix[2] psi;        // covariance matrix among growth parameters.
}

transformed parameters {

real ressd;               // standard deviation of residuals
  ressd <- sqrt(resvar);
}

model {
  vector[N] mu[J];           // temporary variable for expected values

resvar ~ inv_gamma(.001,.001);   // residual variance prior.
  gamma ~ normal(0,1000);          // diffuse prior on intercept and linear growth params.
  gamma20 ~ normal(0,1000);        // diffuse prior on quadratic growth param
  psi ~ inv_wishart(2,Omega);      // prior on intercept and linear covariance matrix

beta ~ multi_normal(gamma,psi);  // prior on level-1 intercept and linear growth params.
 
 
  for(j in 1:J) {
    for(i in 1:N) {
      mu[j,i] <- beta[i,1] + beta[i,2] * time[j] + gamma20 * (time[j] * time[j]);
    }
    y[j] ~ normal(mu[j], ressd);  // growth model. ***
  }
}

generated quantities {
  // real rho;
  // rho <- psi[1,2] / sqrt(psi[1,1] * psi[2,2]);
}

messages.author: 211887b39a900c7d
messages.subject: Re: Estimation Time for Multilevel Model: JAGS v. STAN
parts:
Hi Luc:

Thank you for your recommendations and the vectorized version of the model. Vectorizing the STAN code and moving 'rho' to the generated quantities block reduced the total warm-up and sampling time from ~4.5 minutes to ~2 minutes (for each chain, ~45 seconds for warmup and ~15 seconds for sampling). It takes about 20 seconds to compile the model. The vast majority of the warm-up time is spent on the first 100 iterations in which the inverse wishart prior does appear to produce covariance matrices that are not positive definite; once resolved, estimation speeds up dramatically. Again, thank you for your clear and thorough assistance!

If I may, I do have a couple of follow-up questions about the model compilation. For the simulation study, the sample size from one replication to the next will not constant. Rather, in order to not capitalize on the whims of a specific sample size, I specify a small range of sample sizes when generating data to allow sample sizes to differ between replications. So my questions are the following... Does the compilation of the model depend on the particular sample size? If not, after compiling the model for the first replication, how does one avoid the compilation step for subsequent replications?   

Cheers,

Derek

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: Estimation Time for Multilevel Model: JAGS v. STAN
parts:
Hi Derek,

Glad to help and rewarding to see that the total running time was more than halved.

You don't have to recompile the model as long as the structure is exactly the same. The exact dimenions of vectors and matrices don't have to be the same (though they should probably be at least >1), as long as you haven't hardcoded these somewhere outside the data block.

Just to reiterate: when you have to choose between JAGS and Stan, compare in terms of seconds per effective sample size, not total running time. In the end, you will only need a certain effective sample size. I don't have any recommendations on that (I like being on the safe side and use brute force, but that's not really an appealing option for your simulation study). Some of the Stan Developers may be able to advise on the minimal number of effective samples.

Regarding the Metropolis rejections of the covariance matrices, you can probably gain significant efficiency by modeling it differently. There are several good alternatives in Stan, including modeling the correlation matrix with an LKJ prior, and scaling it with a vector of sigmas (sigma ~ cauchy(0,5) is usually a safe bet, adjust scale to expectation). Alternatively, you could model the sigmas and rho separely (rho ~ uniform(-1,1); this works in JAGS too). You can check the manual for other parameterizations of the multivariate normal. In general, you want to avoid using the "normal" multivariate normal as its evaluation involves computationally expensive matrix inversions (especially for >=trivariate cases) that can be numerically unstable and lead to Metropolis rejections.

Good luck,

Luc

On Aug 3, 2014, at 12:45 PM, Derek Fay <derek.f...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Luc:
>
> Thank you for your recommendations and the vectorized version of the model. Vectorizing the STAN code and moving 'rho' to the generated quantities block reduced the total warm-up and sampling time from ~4.5 minutes to ~2 minutes (for each chain, ~45 seconds for warmup and ~15 seconds for sampling). It takes about 20 seconds to compile the model. The vast majority of the warm-up time is spent on the first 100 iterations in which the inverse wishart prior does appear to produce covariance matrices that are not positive definite; once resolved, estimation speeds up dramatically. Again, thank you for your clear and thorough assistance!

We recommend other priors --- the inverse wishart is only popular
because it's conjugate so used in BUGS/JAGS, which as far as I know
only handle conjugate priors for multivariate quantities.

Having said that, the reason things are slow during warmup is that
Stan is adapting to the scales of each variable for sampling.

The positive-definiteness failures during warmup are usually due to
too large a step size, which will get corrected if warmup converges
to sensible adaptation parameters for step size and diagonal mass
matrix (basically, scale of each variable).

> If I may, I do have a couple of follow-up questions about the model compilation. For the simulation study, the sample size from one replication to the next will not constant. Rather, in order to not capitalize on the whims of a specific sample size, I specify a small range of sample sizes when generating data to allow sample sizes to differ between replications. So my questions are the following... Does the compilation of the model depend on the particular sample size?

Not if it's specified as data. The only time you need to recompile
is when the model changes in the literal sense of being different text.
> If not, after compiling the model for the first replication, how does one avoid the compilation step for subsequent replications?

That depends on whether you are using CmdStan, RStan or PyStan.

Some more comments on the model below.

- Bob

> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> data {
> int<lower=0> N; // Number of subjects.
> int<lower=0> J; // Number of measurement occasions.
> vector[N] y[J]; // Dimensions of the observed data.
> vector[J] time; // Balanced coding of time (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)
> cov_matrix[2] Omega; // Diagonal matrix on growth params (prior).
> }
>
> parameters {
> vector[2] beta[N]; // level-1 growth parameters.
> vector[2] gamma; // level-2 intercept and linear parameters.
> real gamma20; // level-2 quadratic parameter.
> real<lower=.001> ressd; // homoskedastics residual variance
> cov_matrix[2] psi; // covariance matrix among growth parameters.
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
> real ressd; // standard deviation of residuals
> ressd <- sqrt(resvar);
> }

you can define ressd as a local variable in the model if you don't
need to save it and it'll cut down on a bit of I/O.

> model {
> vector[N] mu[J]; // temporary variable for expected values
>
> resvar ~ inv_gamma(.001,.001); // residual variance prior.

These priors can be bad news. I know it was standard practice in
earlier versions of BUGS, but even they are not recommending these
priors any more. We'd recommend using something like a half-cauchy,
as in:

resvar ~ cauchy(0,5);

or even a tighter prior depending on what you know about resvar ahead of time.

> gamma ~ normal(0,1000); // diffuse prior on intercept and linear growth params.
> gamma20 ~ normal(0,1000); // diffuse prior on quadratic growth param

It's more efficient in some cases to take these as normal(0,1) and
then scale gamma and gamma20 by 1000. But adaptation can usually sort
out the scales with a bit of work (the time warmup's taking).

> psi ~ inv_wishart(2,Omega); // prior on intercept and linear covariance matrix
> beta ~ multi_normal(gamma,psi); // prior on level-1 intercept and linear growth params.
>
>
> for(j in 1:J) {
> for(i in 1:N) {
> mu[j,i] <- beta[i,1] + beta[i,2] * time[j] + gamma20 * (time[j] * time[j]);
> }
> y[j] ~ normal(mu[j], ressd); // growth model. ***

You could go even further vectorizing this given that ressd is shared,
and put all of the variables in one big array. Probably won't make a difference
if N is large.

> }
> }
>
> generated quantities {
> // real rho;
> // rho <- psi[1,2] / sqrt(psi[1,1] * psi[2,2]);
> }

If you only use a two by two covariance matrix, then it will be much
more efficient to parameterize the model in terms of a correlation
parameter rho between -1 and 1 and two positive scale parameters,
sqrt(psi[1,1]) and sqrt(psi[2,2]). Then you can put the 2 x 2 covariance
matrix together directly.

The downside is that this only works for the 2 by 2 case.

It's even more efficient to parameterize in terms of cholesky factors,
but I'll stop here. The next version of the manual's going to have
a lot more advice on priors from both a statistical and efficiency
perspective.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Estimation Time for Multilevel Model: JAGS v. STAN
parts:
Let me re-emphasize what Luc says --- only the number of effective
samples per second matters when comparing speed as that determines
the MCMC error (the MCMC version of std error) in your estimates of
posterior means (or other expectations over the posterior).

You've also chosen a particularly easy model for JAGS due to
the use of conjugate priors. Gibbs can be very efficient when everything
is conjugate and there's not too much correlation among parameters in
the posterior. We're not claiming to be faster than JAGS for every conceivable
model.

If Stan converges in fewer iterations, it should also have a higher n_eff
per iteration (i.e., it should mix faster), so you should see a
different story when measuring effective samples rather than iterations.

- Bob
